ai-at-work.title: The most interesting startups right now want to get you off your phone
ai-at-work.excerpt: While the AI fundraising machine keeps breaking its own records, some founders are building in the other direction. Mirror founder Brynn Putnam just raised money for Board, a startup focused on bringi
ai-at-work.dwp_take: A batch of startups are deliberately rejecting the constant connectivity treadmill by building products that push people toward physical interaction and offline activities instead of maximizing screen time. This matters because digital workplace leaders are finally waking up to the fact that Zoom fatigue and notification overload are real problems killing productivity and employee wellbeing, not features to celebrate. After thirty years of watching tech solve problems by adding more tech, it's refreshing to see founders actually admit that sometimes the best digital workplace innovation is knowing when to turn the damn thing off.

ai-at-work.dwp_take: A bunch of startups are deliberately stepping away from AI hype to build products focused on getting people together through analog experiences and in-person interaction. This matters because digital workplace leaders are finally realizing that not every problem needs a machine learning solution and that connection still beats optimization. After three decades watching us chase the next shiny thing, I'm genuinely excited that someone is building toward actual human moments instead of another chatbot.

ai-at-work.title: US government could take stakes in major AI companies
ai-at-work.excerpt: U.S. officials are weighing a proposal that could see the federal government take stakes in leading artificial intelligence providers. The discussions were first reported by news outlet NOTUS late Thu
ai-at-work.dwp_take: The Trump administration is considering having the federal government take equity stakes in major AI companies as a way to secure national interests in the sector. This matters to digital workplace pros because government ownership could reshape which AI tools get preferential treatment, funding, and integration into enterprise systems you'll be implementing over the next decade. Personally, I'd be curious to see how this works out when the same government still can't agree on basic cybersecurity standards for federal contractors.

tools-tech.title: I had ChatGPT build me a free PDF editor because I didn't trust it to change my files - it worked!
tools-tech.excerpt: The smartest way to use AI may not be letting it touch your files, but asking it to write software that handles them safely - in the time it takes to make dinner.
tools-tech.dwp_take: Someone used ChatGPT to generate code for a PDF editor rather than trusting the AI directly with their actual files, and it actually worked. This matters because it highlights a practical security mindset: using AI as a tool builder rather than a black-box processor for sensitive work, which is exactly what thoughtful organizations should be doing. The real insight here isn't that AI is magical, it's that the smartest people aren't treating it like magic, and that's the attitude your team needs before deploying anything in your digital workplace.

tools-tech.title: Tech industry cut 38,242 jobs in May, worst since 2024
tools-tech.excerpt: Technology companies announced 38,242 job cuts in the US in May 2026, the highest monthly total for the sector since August 2024, according to research by employment placement company Challenger, Gray
tools-tech.dwp_take: Tech companies axed over 38,000 jobs in May, marking the worst month for the sector since August 2024, with 2026 already tracking 66 percent higher job losses than last year. For digital workplace pros, this means your organization is probably scrambling to do more with fewer people, which makes efficient tools and processes non-negotiable rather than nice-to-have. The irony is thick: companies cutting headcount while desperately needing better collaboration platforms to keep the remaining staff from drowning in email hell.

tools-tech.title: Microsoft makes Linux developers feel more at home in Windows with Coreutils release
tools-tech.excerpt: Microsoft has announced Coreutils, a new Windows 11 feature that allows developers to run many popular Linux command line utilities natively on Windows from a single binary. Revealed at this week’s Bu
tools-tech.dwp_take: Microsoft released Coreutils, a Windows 11 feature that lets developers run Linux command line tools natively without jumping between environments. This matters because developers increasingly expect seamless cross-platform workflows, and reducing friction between operating systems directly impacts productivity and hiring appeal for tech organizations. After thirty years watching Microsoft chase developer love, I'll believe this actually works smoothly when I see it shipping stable and not requiring seventeen workarounds.

tools-tech.title: What Safari reveals about Apple’s AI strategy ahead of WWDC
tools-tech.excerpt: Apple’s latest Safari privacy campaign is more than pre-WWDC marketing. It is an early signal of how the company plans to frame artificial intelligence (AI): as something that only works if users trus
tools-tech.dwp_take: Apple is positioning privacy as the centerpiece of its AI story, betting that users will embrace AI tools more readily if they trust the company protecting their data. For digital workplace leaders, this matters because employee adoption of AI assistants hinges on confidence that their conversations and documents aren't being harvested for training data. The irony is delicious: Apple's basically saying "our AI is better because we care about privacy" while everyone else is frantically trying to explain why selling user data is totally fine.

digital-culture.title: AI is eliminating entry-level jobs. Education needs to fill the gap
digital-culture.excerpt: As artificial intelligence (AI) takes over many entry-level tasks, early career roles are becoming harder to find and land, with postings declining by 35% since 2023. This decrease has created an expe
digital-culture.dwp_take: Fast Company is reporting that entry-level job postings have dropped 35% since 2023 as AI automates routine tasks, leaving new workers stuck without the traditional on-ramp to gain experience. This matters because digital workplace teams are suddenly tasked with onboarding and mentoring people who skipped the basics, which means your knowledge management and learning systems better be bulletproof. Here's the thing: organizations that figure out how to compress five years of entry-level grunt work into a structured six-month program are going to win talent. Everyone else is going to keep complaining about the experience gap.

digital-culture.title: The job market is bouncing back—but not for these workers
digital-culture.excerpt: The jobs report that came out today held good news for many American workers. In May, employers added 172,000 jobs—stronger than projected job growth—and unemployment did not budge from 4.3%. The leis
digital-culture.dwp_take: The job market is picking up steam with 172,000 new positions in May and unemployment holding steady at 4.3%, driven largely by leisure, hospitality, and healthcare sectors. For digital workplace folks, this matters because it signals which industries are investing in talent and potentially upgrading their tech infrastructure to support new hires and remote work arrangements. Here's the thing though: if you're in tech, finance, or media, you're probably still waiting for your sector to get the memo that hiring season actually started.

digital-culture.title: The ‘AI boomerang’: Why some companies are rehiring employees they laid off due to AI
digital-culture.excerpt: AI-related layoffs have captured everyone’s attention lately. Last month, Meta laid off 10% of its workforce—just months after committing up to $135 billion toward AI development this year. Other comp
digital-culture.dwp_take: Companies that laid off workers while betting big on AI are now rehiring those same people because they realized AI doesn't actually replace the skills they fired. This matters because it exposes the reality that most organizations don't actually understand what AI can and cannot do, forcing digital workplace leaders to rethink their whole strategy around automation and workforce planning. After spending billions on shiny AI tools, these companies are learning the hard way that you still need experienced humans to make anything work, which is humbling for everyone involved.

digital-culture.title: How to showcase your expertise as a strategist, coach, or consultant
digital-culture.excerpt: As a freelance writer, I have it easy. When someone asks for samples of my work, I can send them a link. My skills are right there on the page, with my name on it. But a lot of the solopreneurs in my
digital-culture.dwp_take: Fast Company published a piece about the persistent problem that service professionals face: they can't easily show their work because client confidentiality agreements lock up their best examples. This matters because digital workplace professionals increasingly work as freelancers or independent consultants, and proving competence without exposing client secrets has become a real career blocker. The irony is that strategists, coaches, and consultants often do their smartest work behind closed doors, which means the people who need to see it most are exactly the ones who can't.

industry-news.title: New CISA Warning: Hackers Are Targeting Fuel Tank Monitoring Systems
industry-news.excerpt: CISA warns attackers are targeting internet-exposed Automatic Tank Gauge systems used in fuel storage. Here’s what operators should fix now. The post New CISA Warning: Hackers Are Targeting Fuel Tank
industry-news.dwp_take: CISA just issued a warning that hackers are actively targeting internet-exposed Automatic Tank Gauge systems at fuel storage facilities, and the agency is pushing operators to patch vulnerabilities immediately. This matters to digital workplace folks because critical infrastructure attacks increasingly bleed into corporate networks, and a compromised fuel supply chain can disrupt your entire operation, from logistics to remote work connectivity. The real kicker is that someone thought connecting fuel tank monitors directly to the internet without proper security was a good idea, which tells you everything you need to know about how many organizations still treat security like a decorative houseplant.

Honestly, if you're building internal collaboration tools and not thinking about how they'll eventually coordinate with autonomous systems, you're already behind.

industry-news.excerpt: Broadcom’s AI chip revenue is still surging, but its guidance rattled investors and spilled into South Korea, where Samsung and SK Hynix are exposed to the high-bandwidth memory supply chain behind AI
industry-news.dwp_take: Broadcom's cautious AI chip guidance spooked investors and exposed vulnerabilities in the Asia-Pacific supply chain that feeds the memory demands of AI infrastructure. Digital workplace teams need to pay attention because chip shortages ripple directly into hardware refresh cycles, remote work capacity, and your ability to deploy new collaboration tools. Here's the thing: we've been down this supply chain anxiety road before, and somehow we always figure it out, but maybe this time we should actually plan ahead instead of panic-buying when the shortage hits.
